meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I've missed over 9,000 shots in my career. I've lost almost 300 games. 26 times I've been trusted to take the game-winning shot and missed. I've failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed'?
meta.ogDescription: He said it. He didn't write it. The line is 1997 Nike ad copy by Jamie Barrett — who estimated the 9,000 shots and simply guessed the 26 game-winners.

answer.label: Not Jordan’s line — written for him by Jamie Barrett
answer.authorDates: Advertising copywriter · wrote Nike’s “9,000 Shots” at Wieden + Kennedy, 1997
answer.sourceLine: Michael Jordan really did speak these words — they are his voice-over in Nike’s 30-second spot “9,000 Shots,” widely known as “Failure,” which the Paley Center’s television archive records as first aired on 30 April 1997. He did not compose them: the same catalog record credits Wieden + Kennedy copywriter Jamie Barrett as the spot’s writer, and Gale’s history of the campaign says Barrett wrote the script from his own knowledge of Jordan’s career and worked out the statistics in it himself.
answer.confidenceText: Genuinely spoken by Michael Jordan — genuinely not written by him.

source.excerpt: I’ve missed more than 9,000 shots in my career. I’ve lost almost 300 games. Twenty-six times I’ve been trusted to take the game-winning shot—and missed. I’ve failed over and over and over again in my life. … And that is why I succeed.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced Quotes section for Michael Jordan, in exactly the wording that circulates, citing Robert Goldman and Stephen Papson, Nike Culture: The Sign of the Swoosh (1998), p. 49 ↗. It says nothing about the commercial, or about who wrote it. Quote Investigator has no article on this quote.

The Paley Center for Media’s television archive holds the spot itself as Nike: 9000 Shots {Michael Jordan}, aired 30 April 1997, directed by Mark Romanek, with Jamie Barrett credited as copywriter and Larry Frey as art director ↗.

Gale’s Encyclopedia of Major Marketing Campaigns entry on the campaign, by William D. Baue, transcribes the voice-over and states that Wieden & Kennedy’s Jamie Barrett wrote the script from his personal knowledge of Michael Jordan’s career ↗, estimating the missed-shot total himself and guessing at the game-winner count.

In a 2019 interview Barrett named it the commercial that meant most to him, describing it as one “where I wrote a commercial using Michael Jordan’s words” ↗ — a phrase he leaves unexplained, and which sits awkwardly beside Gale’s account of him inventing the numbers. Whichever reading is right, the writing credit is his.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed in Gale’s Encyclopedia of Major Marketing Campaigns, which notes the final line arrives separately, over Jordan walking into the locker room. The wording that circulates online — and that Wikiquote carries, citing Nike Culture (1998), p. 49 — reads “over 9,000” and “26 times.” Both are transcriptions of the same script; we have not found a rights-cleared transcript from the broadcast itself to settle which is exact.

author.heading: Jamie Barrett
author.metaLine: Advertising copywriter · Wieden + Kennedy, then Goodby Silverstein · founder of barrettSF
author.bio: Jamie Barrett is an American advertising copywriter and creative director who, per Wikipedia, held creative leadership roles at Wieden + Kennedy, Goodby Silverstein & Partners, Fallon and Chiat Day before founding the San Francisco agency barrettSF, now Optimism BH, where he is chief creative officer. The Paley Center for Media’s archive record for Nike’s 1997 “9000 Shots” spot lists him as its copywriter, alongside art director Larry Frey and director Mark Romanek. In a 2019 local-press interview he called it the most meaningful commercial of his career — the credit, in a body of work that also includes ads for ESPN, the NBA and HBO.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: This is the most-quoted “Michael Jordan quote” in circulation, and almost nothing about the way it travels is quite right.

items.why: Quote sites file it as Jordan’s own reflection on his career. It is a 30-second Nike script. Gale’s Encyclopedia of Major Marketing Campaigns states that Wieden & Kennedy’s Jamie Barrett wrote the script for “9,000 Shots” from his personal knowledge of Michael Jordan’s career ↗, and the Paley Center’s archive record credits Barrett as the spot’s copywriter.

The numbers read like a career audit; they are a copywriter’s arithmetic. Gale reports that Barrett estimated the missed shots from Jordan’s career points and rough shooting percentage, and that because missed game-winners were not a tracked statistic he surmised about two a season ↗. Jordan, asked about the 26 at a press conference, said only that it sounded about right.

Two transcriptions of the same script compete: Gale gives “more than 9,000 shots” and “Twenty-six times,” while the version that dominates online — the one Wikiquote carries — reads “over 9,000.” Others have rewritten it outright: PassItOn circulates “On 26 occasions I have been entrusted … And that’s precisely why I succeed” ↗, credited to Jordan with no source at all.

Wikiquote does list the line in its sourced section rather than among misattributions — but it cites a 1998 academic book on Nike advertising ↗ instead of the commercial, and never says the sentence was written by an agency copywriter.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment is one Jordan defended in his own voice; the sentence is an advertisement, first broadcast on 30 April 1997 and credited on the television-archive record to copywriter Jamie Barrett ↗.

context.heading: Why the ad worked
lead: Nike’s “9,000 Shots” ran 30 seconds and was shot over nine hours at Soldier Field in Chicago. A well-dressed Jordan steps out of a limousine and walks past banks of fans, nodding to the custodians and security workers along the way, while his voice-over quietly totals up everything he has got wrong — and only at the locker-room door does it turn the ledger over. Gale’s account of the campaign reports that of all the commercials Jordan made for Nike, this was the one he was proudest of, precisely because it made him look human.

Jordan told Henry Louis Gates Jr., for a profile published in The New Yorker on 1 June 1998, that the idea was “to tell young kids, ‘Don’t be afraid to fail’” — and he had fought the agency for the spot’s plain-spoken direction, telling them to “just show the actual situation.” It landed: USA Today voted it among the best campaigns of 1997 ↗, and it became the first foreign-produced commercial to take the grand prize at the All Japan CM Festival.
context.detailsSummary: Where the numbers actually came from
detailsBody: Gale’s entry reports that Barrett worked the missed-shot figure out himself. He knew Jordan’s career points and approximate shooting percentage off the top of his head, applied simple arithmetic, and landed on roughly 8,000–9,000 misses — a guess that, when he researched it afterwards, “turned out to be on target.”

The “26 times” had no such backstop. Missed game-winners were not a recorded statistic, so — per the same entry — Barrett’s options were to watch every game of Jordan’s career or to surmise that he had failed to hit the game winner about twice a season. He surmised.
Asked about the figure by a reporter at a press conference a few days after the spot first aired, Jordan admitted he could not be sure, and answered: “It sounds about right to me.”
context.pull: “I wrote a commercial using Michael Jordan’s words.” — Jamie Barrett, 2019

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced "Quotes" section for Michael Jordan carries the exact popular wording ("I've missed over 9,000 shots... 26 times I've been trusted to take the game-winning shot and missed..."), cited to Robert Goldman and Stephen Papson, Nike Culture: The Sign of the Swoosh (1998), p. 49, with no mention of the commercial or its writer.

The Paley Center for Media catalog record for "Nike: 9000 Shots {Michael Jordan}" gives year 1997, aired 30 April 1997, 30 seconds, director Mark Romanek, creative credits Jamie Barrett (copywriter) and Larry Frey (art director), talent Michael Jordan, catalog ID AT:49338.013.

Gale's Encyclopedia of Major Marketing Campaigns entry (byline William D. Baue) states: "Wieden & Kennedy's Jamie Barrett wrote the script for '9,000 Shots' from his personal knowledge of Michael Jordan's career"; that he estimated 8,000-9,000 missed shots from career points and shooting percentage and his guesstimate "turned out to be on target"; that missed game-winners were not recorded so he surmised "about twice a season"; that at a press conference days after it aired Jordan said "It sounds about right to me"; it transcribes the voice-over as "I've missed more than 9,000 shots in my career. I've lost almost 300 games. Twenty-six times I've been trusted to take the game-winning shot—and missed. I've failed over and over and over again in my life" plus "And that is why I succeed"; it records the nine-hour Soldier Field shoot, Jordan's remark to Henry Louis Gates Jr. in The New Yorker of 1 June 1998 about telling young kids not to be afraid to fail, his "just show the actual situation" objection to using Oliver Stone, and USA Today voting it among the best campaigns of 1997 and the All Japan CM Festival grand prize.

In this 2019 Piedmont Exedra interview Jamie Barrett says the commercial that was most meaningful to him was "9000 Shots" (released in 1997) "where I wrote a commercial using Michael Jordan's words"; the intro notes he began in advertising in 1985 after Princeton and worked at Wieden & Kennedy, Fallon and Goodby Silverstein, creating ads for Nike, ESPN, NBA and HBO, and launched barrettSF in 2012.

PassItOn displays a reworded variant — "On 26 occasions I have been entrusted to take the game winning shot...and I missed... And that's precisely why I succeed" — credited simply to Michael Jordan with no source given.

Wikipedia gives Michael Jordan's date of birth as February 17, 1963, and his career as Chicago Bulls 1984–1993 and 1995–1998 plus Washington Wizards 2001–2003, with six NBA championships; the article does not mention the 1997 Nike "Failure"/"9,000 shots" commercial.
Internet Archive holds Nike Culture: The Sign of the Swoosh by Robert Goldman and Stephen Papson, Sage Publications, 1998, as a borrowable (access-restricted) scan.

Wikipedia states Jamie Barrett held creative leadership roles at Wieden + Kennedy, Goodby Silverstein & Partners, Fallon and Chiat Day before Optimism BH (formerly Barrett Hofherr / barrettSF), where he is Chief Creative Officer; the page does not mention Nike or Michael Jordan.
